deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a continuous German prose text on Greek history around 460–451 BC. It reads like lecture or reading notes, continuing from folio 84 (the third Messenian war, Cimon's ostracism, the rise of Pericles) and running on to folio 86 (Cimon's last campaign against Persia, the Thirty Years' Peace, the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War). The top right carries page and foliation numbers ('3', '85', and '69' in a different ink).

Content, in order:
(1) Pericles is characterised as a trained orator, builder of Athens' magnificent buildings, and a great general and statesman. He never took a step he might have to retract. He held his position without ever being a member of the Areopagus or archon, and the constitution became more democratic as he rose.
(2) He struggled with the leaders of the aristocrats, named as Tolmides, Myronides and the elder Thucydides, who were able generals.
(3) Events of 457: the Spartans marched to Doris to help the Dorians against the Phocians. They stirred up the Boeotians against Athens, whose retreat was cut off. The result was the battle of Tanagra, in which the Athenians were defeated by the Spartans.
(4) In consequence Cimon was recalled to Athens; the margin gives the date 456.
(5) Cimon planned to resume the war against Persia in order to restore internal concord.
(6) In 451 a truce, a five-year peace, was concluded between Athens and Sparta.

No computation, problem or derivation is present, so there is nothing to restate in modern notation.

The hand is a fluent Kurrent with many abbreviations. The text is consistent with student lecture notes on ancient history, for example in the style of Göttingen lectures such as Heeren's. It is not obviously Gauss's own working hand, and nothing on the page connects to Lagrange or to mathematics, despite the bundle name.
errors: No mathematical content, so no mathematical errors can be assessed.

Historical slip in the notes: Tolmides and Myronides were generals, but they are not usually described as heads of the aristocratic opposition to Pericles. That role belongs chiefly to Cimon and later Thucydides son of Melesias. The 'elder Thucydides' named here is that Thucydides, as distinct from the historian.
The chronology of Cimon's recall varies in the sources: the notes date it 456, while modern accounts often give c. 452/451. Similarly, the 'five-year peace' of 451 is standard.

It contains no mathematics at all, and it may well not be in Gauss's hand (possibly lecture notes by a family member or student). There is nothing here bearing on Gauss's mathematical work.
